13-202.r: Computer chips (integrated circuits / IC chips) → made of Silicon, the substance the book names as newest in chip production; store more data in small space.

13-203.r: ICs are classified by number of transistors: SSI 3–30, MSI 30–300, LSI 300–3,000, VLSI more than 3000.
13-203.h: S, M, L, VL: add one zero at each step (3, 30, 300, 3000).

13-204.r: Modem = Modulator/Demodulator → converts digital signal to analog and analog to digital; it is hardware, not software, an OS or a voltage stabilizer.

13-205.r: Modem → sends and receives data over telephone lines by modulation and demodulation; connects a microcomputer with the telephone.

13-212.r: Fax and email sent through phone lines → use both analog and digital signals.

13-213.r: Decoding → the process by which the receiver interprets the symbols used by the source of the message.

13-214.r: Router, Hub and Switch → all are connecting devices; MPPSC treated the question as a bonus. The book gives no single answer (*).

13-215.r: Router → forwards data packets between computer networks; Switch → connects devices within one network (LAN). The book gives no single answer (*).
13-215.c: No single answer: routers, brouters and gateways can all pass packets between networks, as the explanation shows; the router, option (b), is the standard textbook answer.

13-216.r: Repeater → amplifies the signal to extend the length of a network without loss of signal strength.

13-217.r: Celeron, Pentium and Core series → computer processors (not RAM or microchips).

13-218.r: ROM = Read-Only Memory → data can only be read; non-volatile (keeps contents when computer is off), whereas RAM is volatile.
13-218.t: Don't confuse non-volatile ROM with volatile RAM (Random-Access Memory).

13-219.r: Permanent memory of computer → ROM; its data is not erased even after the computer is turned off.

13-220.r: Non-volatile memory (keeps data when power goes off) → ROM; also flash memory (SSDs, USB drives) and hard disk drives.

13-221.r: Address → the means of specifying the location of data in memory.

13-222.r: CD-ROM = Compact Disc Read-Only Memory → an optical disc; holds up to 700 MB; data cannot be erased and refilled.

13-223.r: RAM = Random Access Memory → temporary, short-term memory; all its data is lost when the computer is switched off.

13-225.r: RAM is NOT like hard disc storage; RAM → temporary, volatile, primary memory, much faster than secondary storage like HDDs.

13-226.r: RAM → primary (internal) memory; Solid State Drive, Hard Disk and USB Pen Drive → secondary (external) memory.

13-228.r: Cache memory → extremely fast, small memory between CPU and main memory; stores data often used by the CPU.

13-229.r: Cache memory (CPU memory) → shortest access time (latency) and highest bandwidth of all storage levels; faster than regular RAM.

13-230.r: Cache memory → fastest memory in a computer; speeds up computer processing; built into the CPU.

13-232.r: Flash memory (pen drive, camera, memory card) → uses less power but is NOT cheaper than mechanical hard drives; costlier per unit storage.

13-233.r: COBOL = Common Business Oriented Language → a computer language.
13-233.h: CO-B-O-L: the B-O is Business Oriented.

13-234.r: ORACLE → database software (DBMS), produced and marketed by Oracle Corporation.

13-235.r: FAST → not a computer language; BASIC (Beginner's All Purpose Symbolic Instruction Code), FORTRAN (Formula Translation) and C are languages.

13-236.r: ROM (Read-Only Memory) → a computer memory, not a language; JAVA, C++ and PASCAL are computer languages.

13-237.r: Paint brush → not a computer language; Basic, C++ and Java are computer languages.

13-238.r: Cobra, Python, Squirrel and Java → all four are computer (programming) languages; Squirrel is Lua-like with C-like syntax; Java created in 1995.

13-239.r: COBOL, PASCAL and BASIC → all high-level programming languages; others: FORTRAN, Java, Python, Visual Basic.

13-240.r: Scientific computer language → FORTRAN (Formula Translation), a high-level language developed by IBM.
13-240.h: FORTRAN = FORmula TRANslation, so it suits scientific formulas.

13-241.r: BASIC → a procedural language; other procedural languages: C, FORTRAN, PASCAL.

13-242.r: Fifth-generation languages (5GL) → focus on AI and logic programming; examples: Prolog, OPS5, Mercury.

13-243.r: JSP = Java Server Pages → builds dynamic web pages; released 1999 by Sun Microsystems; similar to PHP and ASP.

13-244.r: Assembler → converts assembly language into machine language.

13-245.r: Machine language → the only language a computer understands and executes directly; uses only 0 and 1; needs no translator; also called machine code.

13-246.r: Machine language of computer → based on Boolean Algebra, which works with binary digits (bits) 0 and 1.

13-247.r: Digital computer works on the logical principle → binary 1 and 0 plus Boolean logic (AND, OR, NOT) set out by George Boole in the 1850s.

13-248.r: .edu.us domain → an educational institution in the USA (.edu = education, .us = United States).

13-249.r: .com in a website address → Commercial; it is a top-level domain (TLD) in the Domain Name System.

13-250.r: .com, .gov and .net → all valid top-level domain extensions; others: .edu, .org, .info.

13-251.r: Proxy server → intermediary that forwards client requests to other servers; it does NOT provide TCP/IP address (only statement 2 correct).

13-252.r: LTE is marketed as 4G and VoLTE as advanced 4G (not 3G); LTE is not data-only, VoLTE not voice-only → neither statement correct.

13-253.r: VLC (Visible Light Communication) → wavelengths 375–780 nm; sends large data faster than Bluetooth; no electromagnetic interference; NOT long-range.

13-254.r: NFC → contactless, uses electromagnetic radio fields; can use encryption for sensitive data; works at 4 cm or less, not a metre.

13-255.r: Short-Range Devices (SRD) → low-power radio devices; include Closed-circuit TV, RFID and Wireless LAN (all three).

13-256.r: AR → adds digital content to the real world via smartphone/PC camera; VR → shuts out the physical world, complete immersion. Statements 1 and 2 swap them.
13-256.t: Don't swap them: AR keeps the real world, VR replaces it.

13-257.r: Father of Artificial Intelligence → John McCarthy; he coined the term 'Artificial Intelligence' in the 1950s.

13-258.r: 'Imitation Game' → original name Alan Turing gave to the Turing Test, which checks if a machine can think like a human.

13-259.r: Machine learning is a subset of AI; reinforcement learning → trial and error with rewards; supervised learning uses labelled input data (statement B wrong).

13-260.r: Machine Learning → a branch of AI; lets machines imitate human learning and improve accuracy with experience and more data.

13-261.r: Majorana 1 → quantum chip by Microsoft (19 February 2025), not AWS (AWS chip: Ocelot); deep learning is a subset of machine learning.

13-262.r: Sources of AI bias → data, algorithms and people (human interpretation); 'Ability' is not a source.

13-263.r: AI can now effectively → cut electricity use in industrial units, diagnose disease, convert text to speech; not write meaningful stories/songs or transmit electricity wirelessly.

13-264.r: FPGA = Field Programmable Gate Array → an IC that can be reconfigured after manufacturing; used to deploy AI (inference, edge).

13-265.r: 'Maharaja' → Air India's Generative AI virtual agent (2023), powered by Microsoft's Azure OpenAI service; first airline in the world to deploy one.

13-266.r: ChatGPT (Chat Generative Pre-trained Transformer) → AI chatbot by OpenAI, launched November 30, 2022; based on a large language model.

13-267.r: AI Action Summit → Paris (Grand Palais), 10-11 February 2025; co-chaired by India and France; built on Bletchley Park (2023) and Seoul (2024); US, UK did not sign.

13-269.r: Upgraded mobile app 'Suvidha 2.0' → Election Commission of India (October 2024), for candidates and parties to seek campaign permissions.

13-270.r: USB = Universal Serial Bus → most popular connection for digital cameras, printers, scanners and external hard drives.

13-271.r: Port → place on the motherboard where accessories (monitor, keyboard, mouse) connect; interface between computer and peripherals.

13-272.r: Password → protects the computer system from unauthorized access.

13-273.r: 'Finger' protocol → used to find out a user's e-mail address.

13-274.r: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) → digital security infrastructure; creates, manages and revokes digital certificates and manages public-key encryption.

13-275.r: Digital signature → electronic way of signing a document that authenticates the signer and keeps content unchanged; statements 1 and 2 describe a digital signature certificate.

13-276.r: IT Act, 2000 (Section 2 definitions) → Electronic Record, Digital Signature and Certifying Authority (all of the above).

13-277.r: BHIM (NPCI, UPI-based, December 2016) → transfers money to anyone with a UPI-enabled bank account; it has three factors of authentication, not two.

13-278.r: Digital India (launched 1 July 2015) → connect villages to Internet, Wi-Fi in schools, public places, tourist centres; not own Internet companies or MNC data-centre policy.

13-279.r: Aarogya Setu, CoWIN, DigiLocker and DIKSHA → all built on open-source digital platforms (source code open to edit and reuse).

13-280.r: Aadhaar (12-digit UIDAI number for residents) → not proof of citizenship or domicile (Section 9, Aadhaar Act 2016); it can be deactivated or omitted by the Issuing Authority.

13-281.r: Aadhaar open APIs → can be integrated into any electronic device; allow online authentication using fingerprint or iris → both correct.

13-282.r: Blockchain → public ledger everyone can inspect but no single user controls; apps can be built without anybody's permission; data is NOT only about cryptocurrency.

13-283.r: Web 3.0 → people control their own data; blockchain-based social networks possible; run collectively by users, not a corporation → all three correct.

13-284.r: Correct pair: Blockchain → Digital/Cryptocurrency. Belle II → particle physics (B mesons), not AI; CRISPR-Cas9 → genome editing, not particle physics.

13-285.r: Blowfish → symmetric encryption algorithm by Bruce Schneier (1993), alternative to DES; faster, patent-free block cipher.

13-286.r: A computer does input, processing, computing and outputting; it cannot do 'understanding'.

13-287.r: Bug → an error, flaw or fault in a computer program that gives incorrect or unexpected results.

13-288.r: MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) → mainly used by banks to process cheques (special font printed at the bottom of cheques).

13-289.r: OMR = Optical Mark Reader → reads pen or pencil marks on forms; used to check objective-type answer sheets.

13-291.r: IRC = Internet Relay Chat → application layer protocol for real-time text-based chat.

13-292.r: 'G' in 2G Spectrum → Generation (2G = 2nd Generation wireless telephone technology).

13-293.r: CAD = Computer Aided Design → software for precision 2D drawings and 3D models (architects, engineers, artists).

13-294.r: GIF = Graphics Interchange Format → file format for images and simple animation; developed by CompuServe in the late 1980s.

13-295.r: 3D printing → used in confectionery, bionic ears, automotive industry, reconstructive surgery and data processing → all five.

13-296.r: E-governance → technology-driven governance: using ICTs (Wide Area Networks, Internet, mobile computing) in government to enhance governance.

13-297.r: Use of computers in governance to deliver government services → E-Governance.

13-298.r: Four pillars of e-governance → People, Process, Technology, Resources.
13-298.h: Think 'PPT + R': People, Process, Technology, Resources.

13-299.r: Gartner's 4-phase e-governance model → Information → Interaction → Transaction → Transformation.
13-299.h: I-I-T-T: two I's, then two T's.

13-300.r: ICT e-governance → reduces cost of government and increases citizens' input; it does not reduce transparency or increase red tapism.

13-301.r: A computer's strength → its speed, accuracy and memory (all of the above).

13-302.r: Multimedia → graphics, animation, video, music and voice integrated digitally with text.

13-303.r: Multimedia → using more than one type of medium in a computer at the same time.

13-304.r: Multitasking → ability of an operating system to run more than one application at a time.

13-305.r: Telefax → sends text and graphics over telephone lines; fax invented by Scottish inventor Alexander Bain in 1842.

13-306.r: Video mail → can send graphics, video clips and video messages (all of these).

13-307.r: Video conferencing → Internet service for audio and video conversation between participants at different sites.

13-308.r: Video conferencing → video calls using telecommunication technologies; simultaneous two-way video and audio between locations.

13-309.r: Compulsory device for video conferencing → webcam / video camera (input); output via monitor, television or projector.

13-310.r: Video conferencing essentials → video camera, display device, microphone; a telephone is not required.

13-311.r: E-mail = Electronic Mail → sending and receiving digital messages over a computer network.

13-312.r: Two parts of an e-mail address → user name and domain name (username@domainname.extension).

13-313.r: E-mail address: left of @ = username, right of @ = domain name; in mark.sttol@ITdesk.info the domain name is ITdesk.info.

13-314.r: Hotmail, Rediffmail, Yahoo, Gmail → all free e-mail service providers.
